claim: Cerebral cortical architecture at birth encodes regionally differential dendritic arborization and synaptic formation.
source: Cerebral cortical architecture at birth encodes regionally differential dendritic arborization and synaptic formation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a foundational premise of the study.

claim: Cortical architecture at birth underlies behavioral emergence of 2-year-olds.
source: It underlies behavioral emergence of 2-year-olds.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by the prediction results shown in the study.

claim: Brain changes in 0–2 years are most dynamic across the lifespan.
source: Brain changes in 0–2 years are most dynamic across the lifespan.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is consistent with established developmental neuroscience knowledge.

claim: Individual cognitive functions assessed at the age of 2 years were robustly predicted by neonate cortical microstructure using support vector regression.
source: We found that individual cognitive and language functions assessed at the age of 2 years were robustly predicted by neonate cortical microstructure using support vector regression.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by correlation data (r = 0.536, p=1.2 × 10−4) shown in Figure 2.

claim: Individual language functions assessed at the age of 2 years were robustly predicted by neonate cortical microstructure using support vector regression.
source: We found that individual cognitive and language functions assessed at the age of 2 years were robustly predicted by neonate cortical microstructure using support vector regression.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by correlation data (r = 0.474, p=8.8 × 10−4) shown in Figure 2.

claim: Cortical regions contributing heavily to the prediction models exhibited distinctive functional selectivity for cognition and language.
source: Remarkably, cortical regions contributing heavily to the prediction models exhibited distinctive functional selectivity for cognition and language.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the nonoverlapping index of 0.57 and permutation tests (p=0.001) shown in the results.

claim: Regional cortical microstructure at birth is a potential sensitive biomarker in predicting future neurodevelopmental outcomes.
source: These findings highlight regional cortical microstructure at birth as a potential sensitive biomarker in predicting future neurodevelopmental outcomes and identifying individual risks of brain disorders.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the prediction results and stated in the abstract.

claim: Regionally distinctive cortical microstructural architecture profiles around birth result from spatiotemporally heterogeneous underlying cellular and molecular processes.
source: Regionally distinctive cortical microstructural architecture profiles around birth result from immensely complicated and spatiotemporally heterogeneous underlying cellular and molecular processes (Silbereis et al., 2016), including neurogenesis, synapse formation, dendritic arborization, axonal growth, pruning, and myelination.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Disturbance of precisely regulated maturational events is associated with mental disorders.
source: Disturbance of such precisely regulated maturational events is associated with mental disorders (Innocenti and Price, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Diffusion MRI has been widely used for quantifying microstructural changes in white matter maturation.
source: Diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) has been widely used for quantifying microstructural changes in white matter (WM) maturation (e.g. Dubois et al., 2008; Mukherjee et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: dMRI offers insights into maturation of cortical cytoarchitecture because of its sensitivity to organized cortical tissue unique in the fetal and infant brain.
source: Because of its sensitivity to organized cortical tissue (e.g. radial glial scaffold; Rakic, 1995; Sidman and Rakic, 1973) unique in the fetal and infant brain, dMRI also offers insights into maturation of cortical cytoarchitecture.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Cortical FA can effectively quantify local cortical microstructural architecture related to dendritic arborization and synaptic formation.
source: Cortical fractional anisotropy (FA), a dMRI-derived measurement, of infant and fetal brain can effectively quantify local cortical microstructural architecture related to dendritic arborization and synaptic formation.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations in the manuscript.

claim: Increasing dendritic arborization, synaptic formation, and myelination of intracortical axons disrupt the highly organized radial glia in the immature cortex and result in cortical FA decreases.
source: During emergence of brain circuits, increasing dendritic arborization (Bystron et al., 2008; Sidman and Rakic, 1973), synaptic formation (Huttenlocher and Dabholkar, 1997), and myelination of intracortical axons (Yakovlev and Lecours, 1967) disrupt the highly organized radial glia in the immature cortex and result in cortical FA decreases.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Reproducible cortical FA change patterns were documented in many studies of perinatal human brain development.
source: Such reproducible cortical FA change patterns were documented in many studies of perinatal human brain development (Ball et al., 2013; Huang et al., 2006; Huang et al., 2009; Huang et al., 2013; Kroenke et al., 2007; McKinstry et al., 2002; Neil et al., 1998; Ouyang et al., 2019a; Ouyang et al., 2019b; Yu et al., 2016), suggesting sensitivity of cortical FA measures to maturational processes of cortical microstructure.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with extensive citation support.

claim: The first 2 years of life is a critical period for behavioral development, with brain development in this period most rapid across the lifespan.
source: The first 2 years of life is a critical period for behavioral development, with brain development in this period most rapid across the lifespan.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is consistent with established developmental neuroscience knowledge.

claim: Infant behaviors including cognition, language, and motor emerge during the first 2 years and become measurable at around 2 years of age.
source: Infant behaviors including cognition, language, and motor emerge during this time and become measurable at around 2 years of age.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is consistent with developmental psychology knowledge.

claim: Reliable diagnosis for many neuropsychiatric disorders, such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD), can be made only around 2 years of age or later.
source: Reliable diagnosis for many neuropsychiatric disorders, such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD), can be made only around 2 years of age or later (Marín, 2016), as diagnoses rely on observing behavioral problems that are difficult to recognize in early infancy (Arpi and Ferrari, 2013; Ozonoff et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Early intervention for ASD, especially before 2 years of age, has demonstrated potential on improving outcomes.
source: On the other hand, early intervention for ASD, especially before 2 years of age, has demonstrated potential on improving outcomes (Rogers et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Individual differences in brain WM microstructural architectures have been well recognized.
source: Individual differences in brain WM microstructural architectures (Scholz et al., 2009; Yu et al., 2020), behavior, and functions (Braga and Buckner, 2017; Xu et al., 2019) have been well recognized.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Individual variability in brain structures and associated individual variability in future behaviors can be harnessed for robust prediction at the single-subject level.
source: Individual variability in brain structures and associated individual variability in future behaviors can be harnessed for robust prediction at the single-subject level (Kanai and Rees, 2011; Rosenberg et al., 2018), a step further than group classification.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Previous studies have investigated within-sample imaging-outcome correlations, but such correlation approaches made it impossible to be applied to new and incoming subjects.
source: A few studies have been conducted previously to investigate within-sample imaging-outcome correlations (Ball et al., 2015; Counsell et al., 2014; Deoni et al., 2016; Hintz et al., 2015; Keunen et al., 2017; Peyton et al., 2020; Wee et al., 2017; Woodward et al., 2006), while such correlation approaches made it impossible to be applied to new and incoming subjects.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Machine learning approaches that can adopt new subjects and yield continuous prediction values have been explored only recently based on WM structural networks.
source: Machine learning approaches that can adopt new subjects and yield continuous prediction values have been explored only recently based on WM structural networks (Girault et al., 2019; Kawahara et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Association of cortical microstructure with cortical regions is more direct compared to association of WM microstructure with cortical regions through WM fiber end point connectivity.
source: Compared to association of WM microstructure with cortical regions through WM fiber end point connectivity, association of cortical microstructure with cortical regions is more direct.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a logical inference.

claim: Cortical FA predicted neonate age with high accuracy in a previous study.
source: Our previous study Ouyang et al., 2019b demonstrated that cortical FA predicted neonate age with high accuracy.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: dMRI-based cortical microstructure has not been evaluated for predicting either discrete or continuous future behavioral measurement.
source: However, dMRI-based cortical microstructure has not been evaluated for predicting either discrete or continuous future behavioral measurement so far.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction to establish the novelty of the study.

claim: High-resolution dMRI data were acquired from 87 neonates out of 107 recruited neonates.
source: Out of 107 recruited neonates, high-resolution (0.656 × 0.656 × 1.6 mm3) dMRI data were acquired from 87 neonates, of which 46 underwent a follow-up study at their 2 years of age for neurobehavioral assessments of cognitive, language, and motor abilities.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction describing the study cohort.

claim: 46 neonates underwent a follow-up study at their 2 years of age for neurobehavioral assessments of cognitive, language, and motor abilities.
source: Out of 107 recruited neonates, high-resolution (0.656 × 0.656 × 1.6 mm3) dMRI data were acquired from 87 neonates, of which 46 underwent a follow-up study at their 2 years of age for neurobehavioral assessments of cognitive, language, and motor abilities.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction describing the study cohort.

claim: Bayley-III composite scores from 46 subjects at 2 years of age range from 65 to 110 for cognition.
source: The Bayley-III composite scores from these 46 subjects at 2 years of age range from 65 to 110 (mean ± sd: 87.4 ± 8.5) for cognition, 56 to 112 (85.7 ± 10.1) for language, and 73 to 107 (91.2 ± 7.1) for motor abilities (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3a.

claim: Bayley-III composite scores from 46 subjects at 2 years of age range from 56 to 112 for language.
source: The Bayley-III composite scores from these 46 subjects at 2 years of age range from 65 to 110 (mean ± sd: 87.4 ± 8.5) for cognition, 56 to 112 (85.7 ± 10.1) for language, and 73 to 107 (91.2 ± 7.1) for motor abilities (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3a.

claim: Bayley-III composite scores from 46 subjects at 2 years of age range from 73 to 107 for motor abilities.
source: The Bayley-III composite scores from these 46 subjects at 2 years of age range from 65 to 110 (mean ± sd: 87.4 ± 8.5) for cognition, 56 to 112 (85.7 ± 10.1) for language, and 73 to 107 (91.2 ± 7.1) for motor abilities (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3a.

claim: No significant differences between preterm and term born infants were found in any of the Bayley-III composite scores.
source: No significant differences between preterm and term born infants were found in any of the Bayley-III composite scores (all p>0.3; Figure 1—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3b.

claim: No significant correlation between any specific age and neurodevelopmental outcome score was found in either preterm or term born infant groups.
source: No significant correlation between any specific age (i.e. birth age, MRI scan age, and Bayley-III exam age) and neurodevelopmental outcome score was found in either preterm or term born infant groups (all p>0.1; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Supplementary file 2.

claim: Significant correlations between predicted and actual neurodevelopmental outcome were found for cognitive scores (r = 0.536, p=1.2 × 10−4).
source: Significant correlations between predicted and actual neurodevelopmental outcome were found for both cognitive (r = 0.536, p=1.2 × 10−4) and language (r = 0.474, p=8.8 × 10−4) scores, respectively (left panel in Figure 2a and b), indicating robust prediction of cognitive and language outcomes at 2 years old based on cortical FA measures at birth.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Significant correlations between predicted and actual neurodevelopmental outcome were found for language scores (r = 0.474, p=8.8 × 10−4).
source: Significant correlations between predicted and actual neurodevelopmental outcome were found for both cognitive (r = 0.536, p=1.2 × 10−4) and language (r = 0.474, p=8.8 × 10−4) scores, respectively (left panel in Figure 2a and b), indicating robust prediction of cognitive and language outcomes at 2 years old based on cortical FA measures at birth.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: The correlations between predicted and actual scores were significantly higher than those obtained by chance (p<0.005) according to permutation tests.
source: According to the permutation tests, these correlations were significantly higher than those obtained by chance (p<0.005).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing permutation test results.

claim: The mean absolute errors (MAEs) between the predicted and actual scores are 5.49 for cognitive outcomes.
source: The mean absolute errors (MAEs) between the predicted and actual scores are 5.49 and 7 for cognitive and language outcomes respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: The mean absolute errors (MAEs) between the predicted and actual scores are 7 for language outcomes.
source: The mean absolute errors (MAEs) between the predicted and actual scores are 5.49 and 7 for cognitive and language outcomes respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: The MAEs were significantly lower than those obtained by chance (p<0.01) based on permutation tests.
source: These MAEs were significantly lower than those obtained by chance (p<0.01), based on permutation tests.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing permutation test results.

claim: Motor scores were not able to be predicted from cortical FA measures (r = 0.1, p=0.52).
source: However, motor scores were not able to be predicted from cortical FA measures (r = 0.1, p=0.52).
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: Robust estimation of the cognitive and language scores was observed in all prediction models across different cortical parcellation schemes.
source: Across different cortical parcellation schemes, robust estimation of the cognitive and language scores was observed in all prediction models.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing robustness evaluation.

claim: After adjustment for the age effect, correlation between the predicted and actual cognitive or language scores is still significant (p<0.05) with original parcellation of 52 cortical regions.
source: After adjustment for the age effect, correlation between the predicted and actual cognitive or language scores is still significant (p<0.05) with original parcellation of 52 cortical regions.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing age adjustment effects.

claim: Classification accuracy was 76.1% for cognitive scores.
source: Classification accuracy was 76.1% for cognitive and 60.9% for language scores (Figure 2—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2b.

claim: Classification accuracy was 60.9% for language scores.
source: Classification accuracy was 76.1% for cognitive and 60.9% for language scores (Figure 2—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2b.

claim: The area under curve (AUC) was 0.809 for cognitive classifications.
source: Our analysis revealed an area under curve (AUC) of 0.809 and 0.737 for cognitive and language classifications (Figure 2—figure supplement 2c), respectively, supporting the cortical microstructural architecture at birth as a sensitive marker for prediction and potential detection of early behavioral abnormality at a population level.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2c.

claim: The area under curve (AUC) was 0.737 for language classifications.
source: Our analysis revealed an area under curve (AUC) of 0.809 and 0.737 for cognitive and language classifications (Figure 2—figure supplement 2c), respectively, supporting the cortical microstructural architecture at birth as a sensitive marker for prediction and potential detection of early behavioral abnormality at a population level.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2c.

claim: Regional cortical FA measures across entire cortex did not contribute equally to the prediction models.
source: Regional cortical FA measures across entire cortex did not contribute equally to the prediction models.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated by heterogeneous feature contribution patterns in Figure 2.

claim: Right precuneus gyrus (PrCu) showed high contributions in the cognitive prediction model.
source: For instance, from the distribution of normalized feature contribution weights in the cognitive prediction model (center panel in Figure 2a), high contributions from right precuneus gyrus (PrCu) (indicated by black arrow) and bilateral rectus gyri (REC) (indicated by green arrows) are prominent, with bright red gyri associated with high feature contribution.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Bilateral rectus gyri (REC) showed high contributions in the cognitive prediction model.
source: For instance, from the distribution of normalized feature contribution weights in the cognitive prediction model (center panel in Figure 2a), high contributions from right precuneus gyrus (PrCu) (indicated by black arrow) and bilateral rectus gyri (REC) (indicated by green arrows) are prominent, with bright red gyri associated with high feature contribution.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Left postcentral gyrus (PoCG) showed higher feature contribution weight in language prediction model than its counterpart in the right hemisphere.
source: For example, higher feature contribution weight was found in the left postcentral gyrus (PoCG) (indicated by black arrow) than its counterpart in the right hemisphere.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing language prediction.

claim: Left REC, bilateral entorhinal gyrus (ENT), right middle/lateral fronto-orbital gyrus (MFOG/LFOG), and left PoCG are common regions for predicting both cognitive and language outcomes among the top 10 cortical regions.
source: Among these top 10 cortical regions, left REC, bilateral entorhinal gyrus (ENT), right middle/lateral fronto-orbital gyrus (MFOG/LFOG), and left PoCG are the common regions (highlighted in yellow in Figure 3b) for predicting both cognitive and language outcomes.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Right REC, right PrCu, right parahippocampal gyrus (PHG), and left fusiform gyrus (FuG) are unique to cognitive prediction among the top 10 cortical regions.
source: Right REC, right PrCu, right parahippocampal gyrus (PHG), and left fusiform gyrus (FuG) are unique to cognitive prediction (highlighted in red in Figure 3b), and left inferior frontal gyrus (IFG), left cingular gyrus (CingG), left insular cortex (INS), and right angular gyrus (ANG) are unique to language prediction (highlighted in green in Figure 3b).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Left inferior frontal gyrus (IFG), left cingular gyrus (CingG), left insular cortex (INS), and right angular gyrus (ANG) are unique to language prediction among the top 10 cortical regions.
source: Right REC, right PrCu, right parahippocampal gyrus (PHG), and left fusiform gyrus (FuG) are unique to cognitive prediction (highlighted in red in Figure 3b), and left inferior frontal gyrus (IFG), left cingular gyrus (CingG), left insular cortex (INS), and right angular gyrus (ANG) are unique to language prediction (highlighted in green in Figure 3b).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Left IFG, usually known as 'Broca's area' for language production, was uniquely found in the top contributing regions in language prediction model.
source: It is striking that left IFG, usually known as 'Broca's area' for language production, was uniquely found in the top contributing regions in language prediction model.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and is consistent with known language neuroscience.

claim: Right PrCu, an important hub for default mode network, was uniquely found among the top contributing regions in cognitive prediction model.
source: Notably right PrCu, an important hub for default mode network, was uniquely found among the top contributing regions in cognitive prediction model.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and is consistent with known cognitive neuroscience.

claim: The top 10 cortical regions where microstructural measures contributing most to prediction were highly reproducible from 1000 bootstrap resamples for predicting each behavioral outcome.
source: Bootstrapping analysis indicated that the top 10 cortical regions (Figure 3) where microstructural measures contributing most to prediction were highly reproducible from 1000 bootstrap resamples for predicting each behavioral outcome (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The nonoverlapping index between top 10 cortical regions for cognitive and language prediction was 0.57.
source: Distinguishable regional contribution to predicting different outcomes (cognition or language) was quantified by a nonoverlapping index, ranging from 0 to 1 with one indicating completely distinctive regions and 0 indicating same regions. The statistical significance of the observed nonoverlapping index 0.57 was confirmed with permutation tests.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: The observed nonoverlapping index of 0.57 was not likely to be obtained by chance from predicting the same outcome (p=0.001 from testing with leave-one-out resamples; p=0.05 from testing with resamples by randomly selecting 90% of samples).
source: Specifically, the permutation tests indicated that the observed nonoverlapping index of 0.57 was not likely to be obtained by chance from predicting the same outcome (p=0.001 from testing with leave-one-out resamples; p=0.05 from testing with resamples by randomly selecting 90% of samples), supporting distinguishable regional contribution to predicting cognitive or language outcomes.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing permutation test results.

claim: Both cognitive (r = 0.516, p=2.4 × 10−4) and language (r = 0.517, p=2.3 × 10−4) scores can be reliably predicted with WM FA measures.
source: Both cognitive (r = 0.516, p=2.4 × 10−4) and language (r = 0.517, p=2.3 × 10−4) scores can be reliably predicted with WM FA measures, indicated by significant correlations between predicted and actual scores (right panel in Figure 4a).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Solely cortical FA measures at birth are as robust as WM FA measures in predicting the cognitive and language scores at 2 years of age.
source: More importantly, solely cortical FA measures at birth are as robust as WM FA measures in predicting the cognitive and language scores at 2 years of age, demonstrated by similar correlation coefficient values between the predicted and actual scores (Figure 4c, all significant correlation with p<0.05).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Combined cortical and WM FA measures showed higher performance with LOOCV than solely cortical or WM FA measures in predicting cognitive (r = 0.721, p=1.6 × 10−8) and language (r = 0.614, p=5.6 × 10−6) scores.
source: Combined cortical and WM FA measures as features (left panel in Figure 4b) showed higher performance with LOOCV than solely cortical or WM FA measures (Figure 4c) in predicting cognitive (r = 0.721, p=1.6 × 10−8) and language (r = 0.614, p=5.6 × 10−6) scores (right panel in Figure 4b).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 4b and 4c.

claim: Combined features for prediction passed threefold cross validation with significant correlation between predicted and actual cognitive (r = 0.635, p=0.01) and language (r = 0.592, p=0.02) scores across folds.
source: Combined features for prediction also passed threefold cross validation with significant correlation between predicted and actual cognitive (r = 0.635, p=0.01) and language (r = 0.592, p=0.02) scores across folds.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: After false discovery rate (FDR) correction, no significant correlation between motion estimates and FA values of any of 92 brain regions was found.
source: After false discovery rate (FDR) correction, no significant correlation between motion estimates and FA values of any of 92 brain regions was found.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing motion effects analysis.

claim: High performance of prediction models was not affected after statistically controlling for motion estimates in cortical and WM FA measures in the predication models.
source: We also investigated motion effects on prediction results and found that high performance of prediction models was not affected after statistically controlling for motion estimates in cortical and WM FA measures in the predication models, as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Individual variability of cortical microstructure profile around birth can be used to robustly predict the cognitive and language outcomes of individual infant at 2 years of age.
source: In this study, we further demonstrated that individual variability of cortical microstructure profile around birth can be used to robustly predict the cognitive and language outcomes of individual infant at 2 years of age.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the main finding.

claim: This is the first study evaluating regional cortical microstructure for predicting future behavior.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first study evaluating regional cortical microstructure for predicting future behavior, laying the foundation for future works using cortical microstructure profile as 'neuromarkers' to predict the risk of an individual developing health-related behavioral abnormalities (e.g. ASD).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion.

claim: The prediction model is capable of incorporating new and incoming subjects, a step further than previous within-sample imaging-outcome correlation studies.
source: The prediction model is also capable of incorporating new and incoming subjects, a step further than previous within-sample imaging-outcome correlation studies (Ball et al., 2015; Counsell et al., 2014; Deoni et al., 2016; Hintz et al., 2015; Keunen et al., 2017; Peyton et al., 2020; Wee et al., 2017; Woodward et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation support.

claim: High performance achieved in prediction of cognition and language based on cortical FA measures is probably due to sensitivity of cortical microstructural changes to maturational processes including synaptic formation, dendritic arborization, and axonal growth.
source: High performance achieved in prediction of cognition and language based on cortical FA measures (Figure 2) is probably due to sensitivity of cortical microstructural changes to maturational processes including synaptic formation, dendritic arborization, and axonal growth.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Distinctive maturation processes manifested by differentiated cortical FA changes across cortical regions in fetal and infant brains were reproducibly reported.
source: Distinctive maturation processes manifested by differentiated cortical FA changes across cortical regions in fetal and infant brains were reproducibly reported development (Ball et al., 2013; Huang et al., 2006; Huang et al., 2009; Huang et al., 2013; Kroenke et al., 2007; McKinstry et al., 2002; Neil et al., 1998; Ouyang et al., 2019a; Ouyang et al., 2019b; Yu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with extensive citation support.

claim: Cortical thickness, volume, or surface area from structural MRI scans cannot characterize the complex microstructural processes that take place inside the cortical mantle.
source: Although cortical thickness, volume, or surface area from structural MRI scans (i.e. T1- or T2-weighted images) were conventionally primary structural measurements to characterize infant cerebral cortex development (Hazlett et al., 2017; Hill et al., 2010; Lyall et al., 2015), they cannot characterize the complex microstructural processes that take place inside the cortical mantle.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation support.

claim: The underlying microstructural processes quantified by cortical FA may be more sensitive to infants with pathology such as those with risk of ASD compared to macrostructural changes.
source: Compared to macrostructural changes quantified by these conventional measurements, the underlying microstructural processes quantified by cortical FA may be more sensitive to infants with pathology such as those with risk of ASD.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a speculation.

claim: Microstructural measures from solely cerebral cortex or WM at birth have similar sensitivity in predicting neurodevelopment outcomes at 2 years old.
source: Despite the fact that microstructural measures from solely cerebral cortex or WM at birth have similar sensitivity in predicting neurodevelopment outcomes at 2 years old (Figure 4), cortical microstructure is more directly associated with specific cortical regions and thus certain cortical functions, compared to association of WM with the cortical regions through end point connectivity.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figure 4.

claim: Combined cortical and WM microstructural measures at birth offered more baseline information and resulted in improved prediction.
source: On the other hand, combined cortical and WM microstructural measures at birth offered more baseline information and resulted in improved prediction (Figure 4b and c).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figure 4b and c.

claim: During first 2 years after birth, overall size of an infant brain increases dramatically, reaching close to 90% of an adult brain volume by 2 years of age.
source: During first 2 years after birth, overall size of an infant brain increases dramatically, reaching close to 90% of an adult brain volume by 2 years of age (Pfefferbaum et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation support.

claim: Infants start to learn their mother tongue from babbling to full sentences, during the age of 6 months to 2–3 years.
source: For instance, infants start to learn their mother tongue from babbling to full sentences, during the age of 6 months to 2–3 years (Kuhl, 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation support.

claim: Parahippocampal gyrus provides poly-sensory input to the hippocampus and holds an essential position for mediating memory function.
source: Parahippocampal gyrus provides poly-sensory input to the hippocampus (Witter et al., 2000) and holds an essential position for mediating memory function (Young et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation support.

claim: Precuneus is a pivotal hub essential in brain's default-mode network and involved in various higher-order cognitive functions.
source: Precuneus is a pivotal hub essential in brain's default-mode network (Buckner et al., 2008) and involved in various higher-order cognitive functions (Cavanna and Trimble, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation support.

claim: Rectus and fusiform gyri are associated with higher-level social cognition processes.
source: Rectus and fusiform gyri are associated with higher-level social cognition processes (Viskontas et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation support.

claim: Bilateral entorhinal gyri likely serve as a pivot junctional region mediating the processes of different types of sensory information during the cortex-hippocampus interplay.
source: For regions contributing heavily to both cognition and language prediction and painted yellow in Figure 3b, bilateral entorhinal gyri likely serve as a pivot junctional region mediating the processes of different types of sensory information during the cortex-hippocampus interplay (Witter et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation support.

claim: Middle and lateral fronto-orbital gyrus are involved in cognitive processes including learning, memory, and decision-making.
source: Middle and lateral fronto-orbital gyrus are involved in cognitive processes including learning, memory, and decision-making (Wikenheiser and Schoenbaum, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation support.

claim: Left postcentral gyrus with high feature contribution weight in both prediction models is associated with the general motor demands of performing tasks.
source: Left postcentral gyrus with high feature contribution weight in both prediction models is associated with the general motor demands of performing tasks.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation.

claim: The first 2 years of life is a critical and sensitive period for the speech-perception and speech-production development.
source: The first 2 years of life is a critical and sensitive period for the speech-perception and speech-production development (Kuhl, 2004; Werker and Hensch, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation support.

claim: Left IFG, known as 'Broca's area', plays a pivotal role in producing language.
source: It is striking that left IFG, known as 'Broca's area', was identified by this data-driven prediction model because it is well known that Broca's area plays a pivotal role in producing language (Poeppel, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation support.

claim: Angular gyrus supports the integration of semantic information into context and transfers visually perceived words to Wernicke's area.
source: Angular gyrus, another crucial language region in the parietal lobe, supports the integration of semantic information into context and transfers visually perceived words to Wernicke's area.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is consistent with known language neuroscience.

claim: Left insula, a part of the articulatory network in the dual-stream model of speech processing, is involved in translating acoustic speech signals into articulatory representations in the frontal lobe.
source: Left insula, a part of the articulatory network in the dual-stream model of speech processing, is involved in translating acoustic speech signals into articulatory representations in the frontal lobe (Hickok and Poeppel, 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation support.

claim: The high feature contribution weight of insular cortex may be due to its important role in social emotions.
source: Since the Bayley language scale also includes a number of items reflecting social-emotional skills, such as how a child responds to his/her name or reacts when interrupted in play, the high feature contribution weight of insular cortex may be due to its important role in social emotions (Lamm and Singer, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation support as an interpretation.

claim: The high feature contribution weight of cingulate cortex might be related to its key involvement in emotion and social behavior.
source: The high feature contribution weight of cingulate cortex might be related to its key involvement in emotion and social behavior (Bush et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation support as a speculation.

claim: Motor scores from Bayley-III were not predicted reliably possibly due to low variability and low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of cortical FA measurement in primary sensorimotor cortical regions associated with motor function.
source: Motor scores from Bayley-III were not predicted reliably in this study possibly due to low variability and low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of cortical FA measurement in primary sensorimotor cortical regions associated with motor function.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the negative finding.

claim: Cortical FA measurements at primary sensorimotor cortex are relatively low compared to those at other cortices and are barely above the noise floor.
source: Cortical FA measurements at primary sensorimotor cortex are relatively low compared to those at other cortices (Ball et al., 2013; Ouyang et al., 2019b) and are barely above the noise floor, as primary sensorimotor cortex develops earlier compared to cortical regions associated with higher-order brain functions.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation support.

claim: Low functional variability at primary sensorimotor cortex was found in a largely overlapped cohort in a separate study from the authors' group.
source: Low functional variability at primary sensorimotor cortex was found in a largely overlapped cohort in a separate study (Xu et al., 2019) from our group, and was reproducibly found in another cohort (http://developingconnectome.org).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation support.

claim: With strict exclusion criteria of participating cohort around birth, higher average and lower variance of motor scores than those of cognition or language scores play an important role in poor prediction of motor scores.
source: With strict exclusion criteria of participating cohort around birth, higher average and lower variance of motor scores than those of cognition or language scores play an important role in poor prediction of motor scores.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation.

claim: A 'cortical skeleton' approach was adopted to measure cortical microstructure at the center or 'core' of the cortical plate to maximally alleviate the partial volume effects.
source: To maximally alleviate the partial volume effects and enhance the measurement accuracy, we adopted a 'cortical skeleton' approach (Ouyang et al., 2019b; Yu et al., 2016), demonstrated in the Figure 1—figure supplement 4, to measure cortical microstructure at the center or 'core' of the cortical plate.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion describing the methodological approach.

claim: All recruited infants had been rigorously screened by a neonatologist and a pediatric neuroradiologist to exclude any infants with signs of brain injury.
source: All infants had been recruited solely for brain research and rigorously screened by a neonatologist and a pediatric neuroradiologist to exclude any infants with signs of brain injury (see Materials and methods for more details).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion describing the cohort.

claim: No significant correlation was found between birth age or MRI scan age and neurodevelopmental outcomes.
source: As a result, we did not find any significant correlation between birth age or MRI scan age and neurodevelopmental outcomes (see Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with reference to supplementary data.

claim: The effects of premature birth on brain development are considered to be relatively trivial compared with the effects of brain injury and co-morbid condition which was not presented in any recruited infant due to strict exclusion criteria.
source: The literature (Bonifacio et al., 2010) also indicated that the effects of premature birth on brain development are considered to be relatively trivial compared with the effects of brain injury and co-morbid condition which was not presented in any recruited infant due to strict exclusion criteria.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation support.

claim: The prediction model will benefit from validation and replication with an independent infant cohort of a larger sample size for generalization.
source: Despite the fact that relatively high performance of behavioral prediction at a group level was achieved with current cohort of infants, the prediction model will benefit from validation (e.g. k-fold cross-validation) and replication with an independent infant cohort of a larger sample size for generalization.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a limitation and future direction.

claim: Prediction model with individual variability representing a general population from a much larger cohort is warranted in future research before this approach is effective for meaningfully predicting the outcome for a single individual.
source: Thus, prediction model with individual variability representing a general population from a much larger cohort is warranted in future research before this approach is effective for meaningfully predicting the outcome for a single individual.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a limitation and future direction.

claim: Future research will benefit from incorporating distinctive and complementary measurements from multimodal neuroimaging.
source: Future research will also benefit from incorporating distinctive and complementary measurements from multimodal neuroimaging (e.g. Kwon et al., 2014; Smyser et al., 2016), including structural (i.e. T1- or T2-weighted), functional, and diffusion MRI.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation support as a future direction.

claim: The observed neurodevelopmental outcomes were also contributed by unmeasured factors such as maternal age and tertiary educational level as well as other home environment variable following discharge from the hospital.
source: The observed neurodevelopmental outcomes were also contributed by unmeasured factors such as maternal age and tertiary educational level as well as other home environment variable following discharge from the hospital, all of which should be taken into consideration in the future prediction model.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a limitation.

claim: Whole-brain cortical FA at birth could be reliably used for predicting neurodevelopmental outcomes of 2-year-old infants by leveraging individual variability of these measures.
source: In conclusion, whole-brain cortical FA at birth, encoding rich information of dendritic arborization and synaptic formation, could be reliably used for predicting neurodevelopmental outcomes of 2-year-old infants by leveraging individual variability of these measures.
evidence: This is stated in the conclusion summarizing the main finding.

claim: Feature contribution weight in cognitive or language prediction is heterogeneous across brain regions.
source: Feature contribution weight in cognitive or language prediction is heterogeneous across brain regions.
evidence: This is stated in the conclusion summarizing a key finding.

claim: Identifying regions with highest feature contribution weights offers preliminary findings on understanding local brain microstructural basis underlying emergence of future behavior.
source: Identifying regions with highest feature contribution weights offers preliminary findings on understanding local brain microstructural basis underlying emergence of future behavior, enhancing our knowledge of brain-behavior relationships.
evidence: This is stated in the conclusion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Cortical microstructural information at birth may be potentially used for prediction of behavioral abnormality in infants with high risk for brain disorders early at a time when infants are pre-symptomatic in behavioral assessments and intervention may be most effective.
source: These findings also suggest that cortical microstructural information at birth may be potentially used for prediction of behavioral abnormality in infants with high risk for brain disorders early at a time when infants are pre-symptomatic in behavioral assessments and intervention may be most effective.
evidence: This is stated in the conclusion as a speculation about future applications.

claim: A total of 107 neonates were recruited from the Parkland Hospital and scanned at Children's Medical Center at Dallas.
source: A total of 107 neonates were recruited from the Parkland Hospital and scanned at Children's Medical Center at Dallas.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Evaluable MRI was obtained from 87 neonates (58 M/29 F; post-menstrual ages at scan: 31.9–41.7 postmenstrual weeks (PMW); post-menstrual ages at birth: 26–41.4 PMW).
source: Evaluable MRI was obtained from 87 neonates (58 M/29 F; post-menstrual ages at scan: 31.9–41.7 postmenstrual weeks (PMW); post-menstrual ages at birth: 26–41.4 PMW).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: All recruited infants were not clinically indicated and were recruited completely for research purpose which was studying the prenatal and perinatal human brain development.
source: All recruited infants were not clinically indicated. In other words, the infants in this study did not have medical reasons to be scanned with clinical MRI as they were considered healthy in routine medical care. They were recruited completely for research purpose which was studying the prenatal and perinatal human brain development.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: All neonates were scanned with a 3T Philips Achieva System (ages at scan: 31.9–41.7 PMW).
source: All neonates were scanned with a 3T Philips Achieva System (ages at scan: 31.9–41.7 PMW).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: During scan, all neonates were asleep naturally without sedation.
source: During scan, all neonates were asleep naturally without sedation.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: A single-shot echo-planar imaging (EPI) sequence with Sensitivity Encoding parallel imaging (SENSE factor = 2.5) was used for dMRI.
source: A single-shot echo-planar imaging (EPI) sequence with Sensitivity Encoding parallel imaging (SENSE factor = 2.5) was used for dMRI.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Two repetitions were conducted for dMRI acquisition to improve the SNR, resulting in a scan time of 11 min.
source: Two repetitions were conducted for dMRI acquisition to improve the SNR, resulting in a scan time of 11 min.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Diffusion MRI data sets from all neonates were preprocessed using DTIstudio.
source: Diffusion MRI data sets from all neonates were preprocessed using DTIstudio (http://www.mristudio.org) (Jiang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section with citation support.

claim: DWI volumes with translation measurement larger than 5 mm or rotation measurement larger than 5° was determined as corrupted volumes.
source: With occasional abrupt movement during sleep, DWI volumes with translation measurement larger than 5 mm or rotation measurement larger than 5° was determined as corrupted volumes.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing quality control procedures.

claim: The volume-by-volume translation range is 0–1.6 mm with average 0.78 mm and most of translations less than 1 mm.
source: The volume-by-volume translation range is 0–1.6 mm with average 0.78 mm and most of translations less than 1 mm.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing motion measurements.

claim: The volume-by-volume rotation range is 0–0.7° with an average of 0.18° and most of rotations less than 0.3°.
source: The volume-by-volume rotation range is 0–0.7° with an average of 0.18° and most of rotations less than 0.3°.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing motion measurements.

claim: Fifty-two cortical regions parcellated by transforming neonate atlas labels were used to generate cortical FA feature vectors from each participant's dMRI data at birth.
source: Fifty-two cortical regions parcellated by transforming neonate atlas labels (Figure 1—figure supplement 4) were used to generate cortical FA feature vectors from each participant's dMRI data at birth, representing the entire cortical microstructural architecture of an individual neonate (Figure 1; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 1.

claim: An immature cerebral cortical region with highly organized radial glia scaffold is associated with high FA values.
source: An immature cerebral cortical region with highly organized radial glia scaffold is associated with high FA values, whereas a more mature cortical region with extensive dendritic arborizations and synapses formations is associated with low FA values.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and is consistent with known developmental neuroscience.

claim: A more mature cortical region with extensive dendritic arborizations and synapses formations is associated with low FA values.
source: An immature cerebral cortical region with highly organized radial glia scaffold is associated with high FA values, whereas a more mature cortical region with extensive dendritic arborizations and synapses formations is associated with low FA values.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and is consistent with known developmental neuroscience.

claim: For each testing subject out of the 46 participants, the cortical FA features of remaining 45 subjects were used to train prediction models for predicting cognitive or language outcomes of the testing subject at 2 years of age only based on cortical FA of the testing subject at birth.
source: That is, for each testing subject out of the 46 participants, the cortical FA features of remaining 45 subjects were used to train prediction models for predicting cognitive or language outcomes of the testing subject at 2 years of age (right panels in Figure 1) only based on cortical FA of the testing subject at birth.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the LOOCV procedure.

claim: The cognitive scale in Bayley-III estimates cognitive functions including object relatedness, memory, problem solving, and manipulation on the basis of nonverbal activities.
source: The cognitive scale in Bayley-III estimates cognitive functions including object relatedness, memory, problem solving, and manipulation on the basis of nonverbal activities (Bayley, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation support.

claim: The language scale from Bayley-III includes two subdomains: receptive communication and expressive communication.
source: The language scale from Bayley-III includes two subdomains: receptive communication and expressive communication.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion.

claim: The Bayley-III is age standardized and widely used in both research and clinical settings with published norms with a mean (standard deviation) of 100 (15).
source: The Bayley-III is age standardized and widely used in both research and clinical settings. It has published norms with a mean (standard deviation) of 100 (15), with higher scores indicating better performance.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The neurodevelopmental assessment was conducted by a certified neurodevelopmental psychologist, who was blinded to clinical details of infants as well as the neonate MR findings.
source: This neurodevelopmental assessment was conducted by a certified neurodevelopmental psychologist, who was blinded to clinical details of infants as well as the neonate MR findings.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.
